stories.title: Over 300 Christian Brothers served with newspaper summons
stories.summary: The names of over 300 former Christian Brothers have been published in a national newspaper, following an order from the High Court almost two weeks ago. It is the second time in recent months that former members of the congregation have been served with a summons by way of a national newspaper advertisement. The 314 former members have been named publicly as part of a claim for damages for childhood sexual abuse, although it is not being alleged that the men whose names have been published had anything to do with the crimes. In July this year, Ms Justice Mary Rose Gearty separately issued a similar order regarding 341 former members of the Christian Brothers. The move came following the congregation's decision not to provide a nominee for the purposes of litigation in a case in which a man is seeking damages for the sexual and physical abuse he suffered at the hands of Liam Coughlan, a former Christian Brother, at CBS primary school on Stephen Street in Kilkenny in the 1970s. Coughlan of Pine Grove, Tramore, Co Waterford, was jailed in 2023 for sexually assaulting numerous boys at the school during the 1970s, including the man at the centre of the case. He died in prison last month.

stories.title: Are these the biggest tax villains in history?
stories.summary: Analysis: Money may well be the root of all evil, but history has shown that a strong and robust tax system can be an effective first step in disrupting it It is said that "money is the root of all evil", but what about taxation? While history has long recorded the evil acts of the world’s greatest villains, as well as the vast wealth that often flows from their actions, less frequently reported is the role that taxation has often played in disrupting and, in some cases, thwarting that evil. In 2004, Klaus-Dieter Dubon, a retired Bavarian notary and tax expert, claimed to have discovered Adolf Hitler’s tax records, long buried in a Munich archive. These records documented multiple clashes between the German tax authority and the Nazi leader, especially in the early years of his political career. Hitler routinely challenged and delayed paying taxes, despite earning vast sums for speeches, public appearances and even from copyrighting his own image. "He was constantly challenging tax office rulings on his income tax between 1925 and 1932", said Dubon, adding, "He didn't care about their rulings". Dubon also discovered that Hitler had paid no tax on the fortune he earned from sales of Mein Kampf, despite being clearly identified as the author of the infamous book. The tax authority’s efforts were in vain, however. The 1933 Enabling Act not only gave Hitler dictatorial powers, but helped him with his battles with the Munich tax office. By 1935, he was declared free of all existing and future taxes altogether. When the new head of the Munich tax office, Ludwig Mirre, wrote to Hitler seeking permission to excuse him from paying tax, Hitler graciously accepted. Mirre was promoted a month later. "It’s all so ridiculous", said Dubon, "but in a dictatorship, everything the dictator does is correct". In 2005, mere months after Dubon’s discovery, another dictator, Augusto Pinochet, was placed under house arrest in Chile. Together with charges of passport forgery, submitting false government documents and filing a false report on personal assets, Pinochet was charged with evading millions in taxes over many years.

stories.title: Preview: Passivity not an option with victory a must
stories.summary: On the eve of the Republic of Ireland's defeat in Austria, Heimir Hallgrimsson made it abundantly clear where tonight's clash against Kosovo stacked up in his list of priorities going into the final two games of their UEFA Nations League group campaign. "The game against Kosovo is probably, if you look at it, more important for us," the Ireland manager said last Friday in the Raiffeisen Arena's press conference room. Ever since falling to a decidedly dire defeat in Kosovo in September and granting tonight's opponents an all-important head-to-head advantage, Tuesday 17 November at Aviva Stadium was always shaping up to be decisive to one degree or another. However, the head-to-head disadvantage is a moot point in any case now that Kosovo are one point clear of Ireland. Simply put, the Boys in Green have to walk away with all three points to usurp Kosovo and clinch second place. A top two finish has been the stated aim in this campaign for multiple reasons. In the context of the Nations League, the reward for second will be a play-off next March that would offer the possibility of potential promotion to League A for the first time.

stories.title: When words fail, art can start the conversation
stories.summary: 'I wanted to remove barriers to participation and hand the conversation over to people themselves...' Barbara Louise Brennan, founder of Mental Health Matters, introduces the winners of MHM's annual poster competition, celebrating creativity, connection and the power of opening conversations about mental health. In 2008, I reached a point where I no longer wanted to be alive. I survived a life-altering suicide attempt, and the years that followed changed the direction of my life. I went on to spend more than 15 years working in mental-health advocacy, challenging stigma and trying to make conversations about mental health safer, more honest and more human. If you've ever seen a Green Ribbon, you may already know some of my work. For five years, as National Team Lead of See Change, it was my privilege to lead that campaign, encouraging people across Ireland to talk more openly about mental health and challenge stigma. When I eventually went out on my own and founded Mental Health Matters, one message stayed with me: finding the words is not always easy. Sometimes we don't know how to explain what is happening inside us. Sometimes the language feels too clinical or simply inadequate. And sometimes an image can say in an instant what might take paragraphs to explain.

stories.title: Irish cheeses scoop prizes at World Cheese Awards 2026
stories.summary: The World Cheese Awards has just revealed its winners for 2026. Irish cheeses won 20 awards on the night, but one from Co Carlow was voted the Best Irish Cheese for 2026. Mount Leinster Clothbound Cheddar from Coolattin Cheddar in Knockeen in Tullow, Co Carlow was selected by a panel of judges as the best cheese in Ireland. The hard, raw cow's milk cheddar is made with animal rennet and matured for around 12 months. Now in its 38th year, the World Cheese Awards are organised by the Guild of Fine Food and is seen as the most influential event in the cheese industry. The annual competition took place in Córdoba, Spain on November 12, and formed part of the Andalucía-Gusto del Sur International Cheese Festival 2026. It's an especially rigorous event, all unfolding over one day, with scores of tables covered with cheeses laid out for the judges. The event featured 5,330 entries from 45 countries, which were judged by a panel of 270 industry experts from 51 countries in one day of blind tasting and testing.

stories.title: Rents up over 7% in year to September, report finds
stories.summary: Rents for properties which were advertised to let were 7.3% higher in the 12 months to September compared to the same period a year earlier, according to a report by website Daft.ie. Inflation in rents was 4.4% recorded in the same period a year earlier. By September of this year, average monthly rent for properties on the market was €2,239 with prices 43% higher than their pre-Covid levels. The report said inflation for market rents was highest in the cities of Cork (11.3%), Galway (10.3%), Limerick (6.9%) and Dublin (6.3%). Due to rent caps for those who remain in accommodation, rents in the open market are rising faster than those for existing tenants. The report said that since 2016, stayers' rents rose by 23% on average - compared to an increase of 79% seen in the open market.

stories.title: New homes drive FTB mortgage activity in first half
stories.summary: New figures show that the volume of first-time buyer mortgage drawdown rose by 6.6% year on year to a total of 12,567 in the first half of 2026 - the highest half year volumes since 2007. The latest Banking and Payments Federation Ireland figures said the increase was mainly driven by strong growth in FTB mortgages to buy or build new properties across the country, with that number jumping 15.4% compared to the same time last year. First-time buyer FTB mortgages on existing properties rose by only 1%. BPFI said the value of FTB drawdowns increased by 10.5% to €4.1 billion, the highest first half value since the group began the data series in 2003. BPFI said that while growth was seen across most regions, both Wicklow and Limerick saw activity levels fall from recent peaks, down 30% and 16% respectively. Today's figures also show that mover purchaser volumes fell by 4.1% to 3,785, the lowest first half level since 2014.

stories.title: Laws remain headline act despite weekend of excitement
stories.summary: Another week of international rugby matches has brought yet another distraction and focus on the laws rather than the quality of rugby on display. In a week where South Africa and New Zealand have both been beaten by northern hemisphere opposition, the public discourse has been focusing on a hip drop tackle and subsequent citing for Ireland's Sam Prendergast. There is little argument that the hip drop tackle needs to be eradicated from the game. The potential for injury is significant, and World Rugby is right to take action to protect players. However, as another change to the laws surrounding tackle technique comes into effect, there is a question about how quickly players can realistically adapt to what is being asked of them. The new hip drop tackle law was implemented early in November, meaning it arrived in the middle of the season. The definition is relatively straightforward. A hip drop tackle occurs when a ball carrier is tackled from the side or behind, the tackler swings around or through them, and subsequently drops their hips or bodyweight onto the ball carrier's legs or lower limbs as they are brought to ground. The action is now explicitly illegal, with a penalty the minimum sanction. More serious examples, involving greater contact with the lower limbs, can result in a yellow or red card.

stories.title: Are you a gamer? You may be surprised to learn that you are
stories.summary: Analysis: Whether it's a Playstation or Wordle on your phone, chances are you're gaming regularly, even with services that aren't strictly games Do you play games on your PlayStation, Xbox or Switch? What about completing a Wordle or crossword puzzle during your lunch break? Do you take five minutes to play chess or even Duolingo on your phone? If the answer to these questions it yes, you're likely a gamer in some form, whether you realise it or not. It’s unsurprising really. As games have expanded their reach over the last few years, you can now play them almost anywhere. What was restricted to consoles and PCs can now be played on your phone, and companies outside of gaming like the New York Times and Netflix have embraced them too, and for good reason. More than 3.7 billion people play video games globally with revenue generated estimated to be almost $522.5 billion. In Europe alone, 403 million people describe themselves as gamers, which makes up 58% of the continent’s population. When being able to download Grand Theft Auto VI a week before the game is officially released is a news event (with talk of people taking sick leave just to play it), it’s another example of how much of a hold gaming has on the world. stories.title: Eurovision seeks answers over Malaysia LGBTQ+ edits
stories.summary: Eurovision organisers are seeking an explanation after footage appeared to show LGBTQ+ performers and personalities removed from Malaysia's broadcast of the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Martin Green, director of the Eurovision Song Contest, told The Guardian that organisers were "surprised and disappointed" to learn that the broadcast had been altered. He said the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian competition under licence, seeking clarification and asking it to establish with Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why the changes were made. Green said the alterations appeared to have been confined to the Malaysian broadcast, with transmissions in other countries unaffected. The controversy follows Saturday’s inaugural Eurovision Asia final in Bangkok, where footage circulating online appeared to show Philippine comedian and television presenter Vice Ganda removed from the screen while announcing the country’s jury votes. Vice Ganda, who is gay and identifies as non-binary, was shown on the international broadcast awarding the maximum 12 points to Malaysia’s entrant, Aina Abdul.

stories.title: Too dark to run? Easy exercises to do inside
stories.summary: If running is your go-to exercise, it can be tempting to let the darker evenings dissuade you. But there are plenty of great exercises you can do in the comfort of your own home. Personal trainer Henry Myers, who runs Peakonic Training, says runners should maintain their normal training timings, but just swap an outdoor run for indoor movement. "The bigger consideration is protecting whatever good habits and routine you currently have in place," he tells the Press Association. "If you’ve already got a routine that works training into the rest of your lifestyle, start there. "If you normally run at 6pm on a Tuesday, keep that appointment with yourself. Follow your typical routine in prep, as what seems like ordinary tasks are often mental cues that trigger readiness. Your mind will notice the pattern and begin readying you for training – then train, just indoors instead of out." And personal trainer Dean Zweck, head of product at Total Fitness, adds: "Darker evenings and cold, wet weather can make heading out for a run less appealing, particularly after work. Having an indoor alternative can help you maintain a regular routine without having to fit every session around the weather. "Dancing, shadow boxing and short-exercise circuits can all help you work on your cardiovascular fitness at home, making them useful alternatives when you can’t get out for a run. Some people enjoy following a workout, while others prefer putting on music and moving at their own pace.

stories.title: Limerick boxer Lee Reeves dies aged 31
stories.summary: Boxer Lee Reeves has died aged 31, after failing to recover from injuries he suffered in a bout with Gary Cully in Dublin in August. The Limerick man was stretchered out of the ring and brought to hospital after the fight in the 3Arena, with his condition initially described as "critical but stable", before further reports suggested he was making progress. Reeves was moved from hospital in Dublin to Limerick last month to be closer to his family but his condition worsened in recent days. Local media reports in Limerick said he had contracted an infection over the weekend, which led to his death ‌yesterday. A talented amateur, the southpaw turned professional in November 2018, winning his first four fights before a defeat to Artur Davydenko in 2020. His record in advance of the fight with Cully was 16-1 after a victory by knockout against Adras Balogh at Leopardstown Racecourse in June.

stories.title: Nvidia rules out Huang comeback amid return campaign
stories.summary: Nvidia's board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, three people told Reuters, despite a growing campaign for his return days after affairs involving employees and suspected Chinese intelligence ties forced his resignation. More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding Huang's return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump said he would not mindseeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks. The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees - some fiercely loyal to the former CEO - and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain and Washington. Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated yesterday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen." Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him before all the facts are known.

stories.title: Explosive Erasmus comments set the tone for Test week
stories.summary: By naming his team and holding a press conference on Monday, it was always likely that Rassie Erasmus would set the narrative of the week before the clash of Ireland and South Africa on Saturday. His extraordinary claims about apparent double-standards in disciplinary hearings, and a potentially prejudicial prediction about Sam Prendergast's availability for this weekend's game certainly did that. The South Africa head coach was at pains to say he was not "moaning" about decisions, or making any "accusations" about how his team have been treated, but it's likely World Rugby will be getting in contact with the outspoken World Cup-winning coach at some stage this week. With news of Prendergast's citing for an alleged hip-drop tackle still fresh on Monday afternoon, Erasmus was asked whether the availability, or unavailability, of Ireland's out-half would alter how his side prepare for this week. Remarkably, he replied: "My friend, I must say the right words now..." before taking the conversation on a 13-minute diversion. For the first 14 minutes, it had been a vintage, uncontroversial, Rassie Erasmus (below) charm-offensive; the mischievous and witty and magnetic version of the former Munster coach that makes him one of the game's most interesting and at times divisive figures.

stories.title: Schoenaerts given suspended sentence for road offences
stories.summary: A Belgian court has found actor Matthias Schoenaerts guilty of a series of road offences but did not punish him because it said it did not want to harm his US film career. The 48-year-old admitted a slew of traffic offences, including driving while banned, driving while under the influence of alcohol, and driving without insurance. An earlier hearing sentenced Schoenaerts to a six-month prison term when he was not present. A new hearing found him guilty of all the offences but decided to suspend punishment for three years if Schoenaerts underwent road safety counselling and attended a theatre production on road accidents, among other conditions. The court in the northeastern town of Beringen said it did not want to threaten his film career in the United States. "An actual custodial sentence could lead to a ban on entering this country... given the strictness of US immigration law", thereby risking his "social alienation", the court said in a statement.

stories.title: Why Vitamin D supplements are a good idea for the winter months
stories.summary: Analysis: The 'sunshine vitamin' can be in low supply during these dark winter days, which is why many of us are advised to take a supplement When the days shorten and the sun sinks low in the sky, that familiar winter slump sets in. There’s a fundamental reason for this seasonal fatigue: low levels of vitamin D – the "sunshine vitamin". People in this part of the world simply can’t make enough of this vital nutrient from sunlight during winter, which is why many are advised to take a supplement. So, what is vitamin D, why does it matter, and how much do you really need? Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin. This means it’s absorbed with other fats in our diet, and stored in the body’s liver and fatty tissue. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium from the gut and regulates calcium and phosphate levels. These minerals are crucial for healthy bones, teeth and muscles. Vitamin D plays a key role in bone development and in the continuous renewal of bone tissue. Without enough vitamin D, adults can develop osteomalacia (soft bones) and children can develop rickets (a bone deformity, often characterised by bowed legs). Vitamin D supplementation, in conjunction with calcium, helps maintain bone mineral density and has been shown in trials to reduce fracture risk in people with osteoporosis. Many tissues in the body have receptors that respond to vitamin D, as well. This means vitamin D can also affect neuromuscular function by helping us maintain muscle strength. Low vitamin D levels have also been associated with a higher risk of several health problems, including cardiovascular conditions such as high blood pressure and heart failure. However, it’s uncertain whether low vitamin D directly contributes to cardiovascular disease or is simply a reflection of overall poor health in people with chronic conditions.

stories.title: Woman found in Derry bog was killed over 2,000 years ago
stories.summary: An investigation of the ancient remains of a young woman found in a bog in Co Derry has found that she was killed more than 2,000 years ago. The decapitated body was found by workers at a commercial peat extraction company near Bellaghy just over three years ago. A coroner conducted what is believed to be a unique inquest-style inquiry to establish what happened to the woman who was aged between 15 and 22 years old. The subject of the investigation is officially known as Ballymacombs More Woman following a convention that such discoveries are named after the location where they are found. But people in the village know her by a different name. They have named her after a mythical Goddess called Áine. The coroner’s findings about what happened to her were delivered at a public hearing in the Ulster Museum in Belfast yesterday.

stories.summary: British wage growth slowed in the third quarter of this year against a backdrop of the biggest fall in job vacancies in over ⁠a year, but the jobless rate also dropped, giving a mixed picture of inflation pressures in the UK job market. This was slightly below economists' median forecast of 3.6% in a Reuters poll and down from growth of 3.7% in the three months to August. stories.title: Idah: Ireland have learned lessons from last Kosovo clash
stories.summary: Adam Idah believes that the Republic of Ireland have learned lessons from their last clash with Kosovo ahead of the side's UEFA Nations League meeting in Dublin tonight. The Boys in Green were beaten 1-0 in Pristina in September which leaves them needing a victory to secure second place in group B3, and the chance at promotion that comes with it via the play-offs. Defeat could lead to a play-off of another kind, namely potential relegation to League C. For that to happen, another loss to the Kosovans would have to be coupled with a victory for Israel over already promoted Austria. Idah says that discussions have taken place around the set up against Kosovo last time, and that changes have been made. "The last couple of games, we really went for it and we were able to show teams what we're capable of. Me, Troy and Jack, we really work together well and do it out in training. "So, we're really enjoying it; hopefully, we can just get some wins."

stories.title: Russia says it carried out major strikes on Ukraine
stories.summary: Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities and transport infrastructure in a number of regions. The strikes hit Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia as well as the Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions. The ministry said energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels used by Ukraine's armed forces were also targeted. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, along with some other critical infrastructure. "According to preliminary information, there have been hits on the North and South bridges in the capital," Mr Klitschko wrote on Telegram. The attack partially damaged the subway system, prompted some water and power cuts and traffic restrictions. Witnesses reported a series of loud explosions in the capital. Earlier this month and in October, Russian forces had also launched attacks on bridges crossing the river.

stories.title: Thornton confident Ireland can make Swiss statement
stories.summary: Ireland captain Edel Thornton has urged her team-mates to "disrupt their opponents on both ends of the floor" when they take on Switzerland in FIBA Women's EuroBasket 2029 Qualifying in Fribourg this evening. The Swiss are ranked 30 places above Ireland in FIBA's world rankings. Ireland come into this game off the back of a convincing 91-73 win over Azerbaijan in Baku on Saturday, making it two wins in their last three away games in the process. Thornton wants the squad to harness those previous experiences in what will be another hostile atmosphere. "I think over the past couple of years that belief in the group has definitely continued to grow," she said. "This is a bit of a new group in a sense, but we all firmly believe that if we put our best foot forward that the result will take care of itself. This is just a great opportunity for us to take another step forward as a group with this style of basketball that we're trying to execute in each game and just enjoy ourselves in the process."

stories.summary: The Republic ff Ireland may have went out on their shield following a gutsy display against Austria on Saturday night - but the Boys in Green need to tighten up at the back if they're to grab a much-needed win against Kosovo this evening, according to former international Keith Treacy. A scrappy goal finished from close range by Austrian substitute Sasa Kalajdzic with little more than 10 minutes remaining nobbled Heimir Hellgrimsson's side in Linz after some resolute defending - and a few fine saves from goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher - had looked like giving Ireland a precious point on the road. "After the game, Heimir is talking about how we're defending well - I'm not so sure we did defend well," Treacy argued. "With the players we have available in our defence, our currency should be clean sheets. If we keep clean sheets then we've defended well." While Ireland also had their chances to nick a goal at the other end - Troy Parrott going close a number of times and home keeper Alexander Schlager making a string of saves of his own - the fact Brentford stopper Kelleher was ultimately named Man of the Match is indicative of how much of the ball Austria had, particularly in the second half. "To give up an xG of just over two to Austria away from home - it's not good enough," Treacy continued.

stories.title: Nearly 73% do not trust Black Friday prices, survey finds
stories.summary: Nearly three quarters (73%) of consumers do not trust that Black Friday discounted prices are accurate, new research has found. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), which carried out the study among 1,028 consumers in Ireland, said the figure is the lowest level of trust since it began gathering consumer research on Black Friday in 2022 (when 61% did not trust Black Friday sales prices). The CCPC also found that four out of five shoppers will do research to check if discounts are accurate before buying. Meanwhile, the study suggests that average spend among shoppers has fallen to €307 (from a high of €431 in 2024), while nearly half of consumers (47%) say the cost of living has made them less likely to shop in Black Friday sales. However, over a quarter of respondents (26%) said the cost of living "will make them more likely to shop in the Black Friday sales". According to the consumer watchdog, men expect to spend more than women (€356 vs €269), but women say they are more likely to purchase something during the sales (38% vs 31%).

stories.title: Republic of Ireland v Kosovo: All you need to know
stories.summary: It's forecast to be showery throughout the day in Dublin with highest temperatures of 7-12C and moderate winds. Heimir Hallgrimsson was relatively upbeat after his side fell to a 1-0 loss in Austria on Saturday night thanks to a late goal from beanpole striker Sasa Kalajdzic. Pre-match, Hallgrimsson was energised by "a sexy lineup" and he was able to take some positives from the patterns of play Troy Parrott, Jack Moylan, Adam Idah and Finn Azaz knitted together at times. But there were issues too. After a bright opening half, Ireland lost control after the hour mark, and failed to adjust when Ralf Rangnick threw on 6'7" target man Kalajdzic. Giving up a soft goal in the later stages of a contest is an annoying habit that Ireland are struggling to kick. The loss ended Irish hopes of topping the group and they now head for a must-win showdown against Kosovo with promotion still up for grabs. A victory at Lansdowne Road would secure second place and send the Boys in Green into a promotion/relegation play-off against a League A country in March. Defeat could condemn Ireland to a play-off to avoid relegation to League C, if Israel manage to beat Austria in Debrecen.

stories.title: Australia eases backpacker visa curbs after backlash
stories.summary: More backpackers will be able stay in Australia on working holiday visas but they will need to work longer in rural towns, the government said, in a softening of planned migration curbs. Under pressure from the rising popularity of far-right party One Nation and housing shortages, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's Labor Party government pledged in September to lower migration. But cuts to tens of thousands of visas for young working holidaymakers prompted a backlash from rural employers that rely on backpackers on farms for fruit picking and for restaurant and tourism jobs. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the planned cap on working holidaymakers wanting to stay in Australia for a third year would lift from 5,000 places to 25,000 next year. The increase represents a smaller cut to the 31,000 third-year visas granted in 2025. The rural work requirement for a second year visa, capped at 45,000 places, or a 20% cut, from last year, will increase from three months to four months.

stories.title: Erasmus makes extraordinary double-standard claims
stories.summary: South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus says he believes Sam Prendergast will be free to take on the Springboks this Saturday, suggesting the out-half will escape a suspension for an alleged hip-drop tackle due to a "technicality". In an extraordinary press conference ahead of Saturday's meeting between the sides at Aviva Stadium, Erasmus took aim at the officiating of his side's defeat to France last Friday, while also expressing his belief that there have been double-standards around how his players have been dealt with in disciplinary procedures. Ireland's Prendergast was cited for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Fijian captain Peceli Yato in Saturday's 43-15 win against Fiji, with the out-half becoming the first player to be cited for the offence which World Rugby has outlawed since this month. stories.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial over killing of children
stories.summary: A judge in the US has set a second trial for Linsday Clancy for 29 March after a jury deadlocked in her initial trial on murder charges for killing her three young children at her home in 2023, in a case that ignited debates over postpartum mental illness. Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, declared a mistrial on 4 September after a single holdout juror prevented a 12-member jury from reaching a unanimous verdict. Her lawyer at the first trial argued she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she killed her children. The judge last week largely sided with the prosecution on those motions, including by rejecting Ms Clancy's argument that the case should be dismissed because a second trial would violate her constitutional rights. Ms Clancy, 36, faced first-degree murder charges over the deaths of her daughter Cora, 5; son Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old son Callan. If convicted of those charges, she would be sentenced to life in prison without parole.

stories.title: EU nations unveil Rwanda deal for migrant return hub
stories.summary: Five EU countries including Germany, Austria and Denmark have unveiled a deal to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda-the first such facility outside the bloc. The initiative, which has drawn criticism from human rights groups, was presented at a press conference in Vienna, with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker saying the group planned to "open the first return centre in Rwanda in 2027". The group, which also comprises Greece and the Netherlands, has been pushing to open a "return-hub" after the European Union cleared the way with a recent toughening of migration rules. Rwanda had confirmed in August it had begun "preliminary discussions" with several European states. Prior to the press conference, ministers from the five EU countries gathered at the interior ministry in Vienna for a "working session". Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan spoke at the event in Vienna.
